clinicalPearls: The classic triad is a quotidian (once- or twice-daily spiking) fever, an evanescent salmon-pink rash that appears with fever peaks, and arthritis, though joint involvement may lag behind the systemic features
Regarded as an autoinflammatory rather than a classically autoantibody-driven disease, so antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor are typically negative and unhelpful diagnostically
Markedly raised inflammatory markers, neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, anaemia of inflammation and a strikingly high serum ferritin are characteristic
Serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis), hepatosplenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy are common systemic accompaniments

Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life-threatening complication signalled by falling cell counts, falling erythrocyte sedimentation rate with rising ferritin, hypofibrinogenaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and hepatic dysfunction
IL-1 and IL-6 blockade have transformed management and are used early in systemic disease, alongside systemic corticosteroids for severe presentations
Chronic anterior uveitis is uncommon in the systemic subtype compared with oligoarticular disease, but ophthalmology review remains part of overall JIA surveillance
A biphasic course is described, with an early systemic-inflammatory phase and a later chronic destructive arthritis phase in a subset of children
reference.pathophysiology: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis is best understood as an autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulated innate immunity rather than adaptive autoimmunity. Excess production of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and interleukin-18, together with activated neutrophils and macrophages, produces the systemic features of fever, rash, serositis and reticuloendothelial activation. Uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation can tip into a cytokine storm known as macrophage activation syndrome, a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Persistent joint inflammation in the chronic phase may reflect a shift towards adaptive immune mechanisms and can lead to erosive, destructive arthritis if inadequately controlled.
additionalDifferentials: Leukaemia or lymphoma presenting with fever and cytopenias
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue disease
Inflammatory bowel disease with systemic features
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with differential looking for neutrophilia, thrombocytosis and anaemia (and cytopenias suggesting MAS)
Inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Serum ferritin, fibrinogen, triglycerides and liver function tests to detect macrophage activation syndrome
Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor (usually negative) to help exclude other subtypes and connective tissue disease
Blood cultures and infection screen, plus bone marrow examination when malignancy or HLH is a concern
Echocardiography and chest imaging when serositis is suspected
Slit-lamp ophthalmology assessment as part of JIA uveitis surveillance
redFlags: Falling blood counts, rising ferritin and falling erythrocyte sedimentation rate suggesting macrophage activation syndrome
Bleeding, encephalopathy or multiorgan dysfunction indicating severe MAS
Cardiac tamponade from large pericardial effusion
Cytopenias, bone pain or blast cells raising concern for underlying malignancy
Persistent unexplained fever with clinical deterioration despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Outcomes have improved substantially with early cytokine-targeted therapy; some children achieve durable remission, whereas others develop persistent destructive polyarthritis or recurrent systemic flares. Macrophage activation syndrome carries appreciable mortality and requires prompt recognition and intensive immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Attributing persistent fever and raised inflammatory markers to infection and delaying rheumatological assessment
Overlooking evolving macrophage activation syndrome when the erythrocyte sedimentation rate paradoxically falls
Assuming a negative antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor exclude the diagnosis
Failing to exclude leukaemia before starting corticosteroids in a febrile child with cytopenias
Neglecting long-term monitoring for growth impairment and joint damage
references: ILAR classification of juvenile idiopathic arthritis
PRINTO/PReS consensus on systemic JIA and MAS
management: Early cytokine-targeted biologic therapy with interleukin-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) or interleukin-6 blockade (tocilizumab) as the disease-modifying mainstay
Systemic corticosteroids for severe systemic presentations and to bridge to biologic control
NSAIDs for symptomatic relief of fever and arthralgia in milder disease
Methotrexate or continued biologic therapy for persistent, potentially erosive arthritis
Vigilance for macrophage activation syndrome, treated urgently with high-dose corticosteroids, anakinra and ciclosporin
Monitoring of growth, bone health, and drug toxicity, with physiotherapy to preserve joint function
Management within a paediatric rheumatology multidisciplinary team
